summary: Describes the architecture of Internet email, which has grown in scale and complexity over decades while evolving rather than being replaced. It gives a common vocabulary for the components and roles involved, so people can discuss the system consistently. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Email passes through many helpers on its way. This is a map naming each helper and what it does, so everyone can talk about the system using the same words.

questions: what is the internet mail architecture

subtitle: A shared vocabulary and map of the roles, identities and components that make Internet email work.

tldr.problem: Internet Mail grew over thirty-five years into a large, complex global service, and people working on it often use different models and different meanings for the same terms.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the current architecture after the fact: who the Actors are (Users, the Message Handling Service and administrative domains), what identities a message carries, and which components (MUA, MSA, MTA, MDA, Message Store) do which job.
tldr.outcome: It gives collaborators one common frame of reference. It introduces no new protocol and imposes no new requirements.

today: RFC 5598 is an Informational document, published in July 2009, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the architecture and sets no standard.

sections.title: Why an Architecture Document
sections.content:
Over its thirty-five-year history, Internet Mail has changed significantly in scale and complexity. The changes were evolutionary rather than revolutionary, reflecting a strong desire to preserve the installed base. Three specifications form the core: SMTP moves a message through the Internet, the Internet Mail Format (IMF) defines the message object, and MIME adds multimedia attachments.

The motivation is practical. Public collaboration on technical, operational and policy work, including work against email abuse, has brought in many participants, and discussions are hindered by different models of email-service design and different meanings for the same terms. The RFC describes the service as it is, post hoc, and says that variance of a protocol from the architecture is not a mark against the protocol: the IETF prefers running code to architectural purity.

The oldest model splits the world into the user side, with Message User Agents (MUAs), and the transfer side, the Message Handling Service (MHS), built from Message Transfer Agents (MTAs). Mail needs no prior arrangement between independent operators, and the Author and Recipient need not be online at the same time.
sections.eli5: Email has been around a long time and many people built different parts of it. This document gives all the parts agreed names so grown-ups stop talking past each other.

sections.title: Actors and Their Roles
sections.content:
The RFC sorts participants into three kinds of Actor: Users, the Message Handling Service (MHS) and ADministrative Management Domains (ADMDs). As a rule of thumb, User Actors can generate, modify or look at the whole message, while MHS Actors work only with transfer data.

There are four types of User: the Author who creates the message and its recipient list, the Recipient who consumes it, the Return Handler (also called the Bounce Handler) who services notifications about failures or completions, and the Mediator who receives, reformulates and redistributes messages, as a mailing list does.

Inside the MHS, the Originator checks that a message is valid and submits it to a Relay, the Relay does store-and-forward routing and adds trace information, the Gateway connects to a different kind of mail service, and the Receiver performs final delivery. An ADMD is a group under one administrative authority, such as a department, an enterprise IT group or an ISP. The three basic types are Edge, Consumer and Transit.

When a Relay gives up on a message it becomes an Author, because it sends an error message to the Return Address. To avoid loops, that error message carries no Return Address.
sections.eli5: Think of a letter: someone writes it, a post office handles it, and someone reads it. Some helpers, like a club secretary who copies a note to every member, write a brand new letter based on yours.

sections.title: Identities in a Message
sections.content:
Internet Mail uses four forms of identity: the mailbox, the domain name, the message identifier and the ENVID (envelope identifier). A mailbox is an address in two parts separated by an at-sign. The right side is a domain name tied to an ADMD. The left side, the local-part, is opaque to the world and interpreted only by the domain named on the right.

Two tags identify messages. The Message-ID: pertains to content, is assigned by the Originator and is globally unique. Whether a changed message gets a new one is a subjective call: a message changed only in form is still the same message, while a forwarded message is a new one. The Message-ID is not meant for anything with security implications. The ENVID pertains to transfer and labels a single transit through the MHS.

Different layers carry different address fields, set by different Actors. The envelope address RFC5321.MailFrom is not necessarily the Author. It is the address to be informed about transfer-level problems. The IP source address is often treated as authoritative, but false addresses are possible.
sections.eli5: An email address is like a street address, with a house name on the left and a town on the right. Only the town knows what the house name means. Every letter also gets a tracking label so it can be found.

sections.title: Components and Protocols
sections.content:
The architecture has six basic types of functionality arranged to support store-and-forward: the Message, the Message User Agent (MUA), the Message Submission Agent (MSA), the Message Transfer Agent (MTA), the Message Delivery Agent (MDA) and the Message Store (MS). A message is an envelope used by the MHS plus content, which is a header and a body. The body may be plain text or a tree of MIME body parts, popularly called attachments.

The Author MUA creates a message and posts it to an MSA. Posting has historically used SMTP, and the currently preferred standard is SUBMISSION (RFC 4409), which uses a separate TCP port and has distinct requirements such as access authorization. The MSA enforces local policy and Internet standards and may add fields such as Date: and Message-ID:.

MTAs relay the message hop by hop, mainly with SMTP (RFC 5321). An MTA does not change envelope addresses or the editorial content, but it adds trace information. The dominant routing mechanism is the DNS MX record. Unlike typical packet switches, MTAs are expected to store messages so they survive interruptions. Finally the MDA performs delivery into the Recipient's environment, and the MUA reads from the Message Store using POP or IMAP.

Mail normally follows a push model, where the holder initiates the next transfer. Pull-based transfer exists too, with ETRN and ODMR. The RFC also stresses that an implementation may combine or separate these modules freely.
sections.eli5: You hand your letter to a post office counter, trucks carry it from depot to depot, and a local carrier puts it in the right box. Each stop has one job and passes the letter along.

sections.title: Mediators: Aliases, Resenders, Lists and Gateways
sections.content:
A Mediator re-posts a message through a new posting, so the MHS sees a new message, but readers still see it as coming from, or at least started by, the original Author. This differs from basic MTA relaying, which has no freedom to change addressing or content.

  • Alias: a simple re-addressing step, normally part of an MDA, that changes only the envelope recipient. The original return address is kept, so delivery problems go to the original Author, who may not know the alias exists.
  • ReSender: splices the addressing so the new Recipient can reply directly to the original Author, using the Resent-* header fields.
  • Mailing List: an elaboration of the ReSender that re-posts to subscribers, may change content and archives messages. It becomes the Author of the new message and sets the return address.
  • Gateway: may change content, structure or addresses to cross into a service with different standards. This almost always loses some meaning. A good test is whether a Recipient can automatically formulate a valid reply.

Organizations may also run a Boundary Filter that checks messages against safety policy, for example to detect spam or viruses, and may alter the content to make it safe.
sections.eli5: A Mediator is like a club secretary who gets your note and passes copies to every member. It still looks like it came from you, but the secretary is now responsible for sending it.

sections.title: Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
This document introduces no new capabilities. The core of the architecture imposes no security requirements on either end-to-end or hop-by-hop components: it does not require participant authentication and does not try to prevent disclosure. Security mechanisms live in other specifications, such as SMTP-TLS, SMTP-Auth, OpenPGP and S/MIME. The RFC notes that spam is a by-product of an architecture designed for open and casual exchange, and that using the IP source address for policy decisions is common but risky because it can be spoofed.

On internationalization, the core email standards are based on 7-bit US-ASCII. They have been enhanced incrementally: MIME allows other character sets and content transfer encodings, an SMTP option allows 8-bit text, and experimental Email Address Internationalization work allows UTF-8 in addresses and header fields. The RFC concludes that the use of UTF-8 is fully established in existing Internet Mail.
sections.eli5: The mail system was built so anyone can send to anyone, which is friendly but not very guarded. Locks like encryption exist, but they are separate add-ons, and the system now also handles letters in many alphabets.
